chapter_theme: The venbas Pattinathar is said to have sung while performing his mother's cremation: ten months of carrying, the breast, the cradle, the shoulder, the voice that called him honey and nectar, set against the firebrand he must now put to her head and the rice he must put in her mouth. The renunciant who has disowned every bond finds the one debt he cannot repay, and the series ends by naming the four fires, Tripura, Lanka, the fire she lit in his belly and the one he lights, and by declaring that the mother who sat in state yesterday and is ash today is, like everything, Siva.
structure_note: The editorial heading on 390 to 395 (தாயாருக்குத் தகனகிரியை செய்கையிற் பாடிய வெண்பா) is a modern editor's, as are the metre labels. 390 to 393 are four parallel venbas, each a list of what the mother did ending in the question of what the son now does (தீ மூட்டுவேன்); 394 and 395 are a pair on the mouth-rice and the firebrand; 396 is a single viruttam of four fires; 397 to 399 move from the burning to the question of where she went to the closing எல்லாம் சிவமயம்.

390.reading: For ten months, every limb aching, she bore and gave birth, and the moment they said 'a boy' she lifted me with care in her two red hands and gave me her golden breast: in what birth shall I see her again?
390.nuance: The closing question, எப்பிறப்பிற் காண்பேன், is not answered; it can be grief (never again) or the renunciant's literal doubt whether any birth will bring her back. The verse itself only counts what she gave.

391.reading: She first lay in penance, then carried me three hundred days, worshipped Siva day and night, and bore me with her belly sagging as she carried: for that mother am I to kindle the burning flame?
391.nuance: முந்தித் தவங்கிடந்து is the penance undertaken for a child before conception, so the mother's giving begins before the pregnancy. The question தமக்கோ எரியத் தழல் மூட்டுவேன் is rhetorical in form but the son does light the fire; the verse is the cost, not a refusal.

392.reading: In the dish, in the cradle, on her chest, on her shoulder and on the bed she set me and loved me, folded me under her wing and guarded me and dandled me: for that mother am I to set fire to the firewood?
392.nuance: The five places are the stages of an infant's day, and சிறகிலிட்டு, under the wing, makes the mother a bird. The venba's second half repeats 391's turn to the pyre almost word for word; the four verses vary the list and keep the question.

393.reading: She bore me in pain and gave birth, held me so I would not hurt, gave the breast, raised me and lifted me without tiring, carried me in her arms day and night and kept me safe: for that mother am I to set fire to her body?
393.nuance: மெய்யிலே தீ மூட்டுவேன், fire to the body itself, is the barest of the four endings; the earlier verses said the flame or the firewood. The progression across 391 to 393 moves the fire closer to her.

394.reading: Am I to put rice into the mouth that, without taking pleasure in setting out portions and sharing them, called me 'honey, nectar, wealth, treasure, my deer': is that the rice I shall give?
394.nuance: அரிசி இடுதல் is the funeral rite of placing rice in the corpse's mouth (வாய்க்கரிசி); the verse turns on the irony that the mouth which fed him with names now receives a handful of raw grain. Line 2, வரிசையிட்டுப் பாத்து மகிழாமல், is hard: it may mean she did not stop to portion food out for others, giving all to him, or that she took no pleasure in being served herself.

395.reading: Is it rice that I scoop and put in, mother? Shall I set the firebrand on your head without flinching, on the mouth that softly laid face against face, kissed me and called 'my son'?
395.nuance: The pair of 394, now with the firebrand (கொள்ளி) added to the rice; கூசாமல், without shrinking, is the one word for the son's own state, and it is a question. The two rites, rice and fire, are the chief mourner's duties, and the eldest son's.

396.reading: The fire set of old on the three cities, the fire set afterwards on southern Lanka, the fire my mother set in the pit of my belly, and the fire I now set: let them all blaze, let them blaze.
396.nuance: Two fires are the gods' (Siva's at Tripura, Hanuman's at Lanka) and two are the family's. அன்னை இட்ட தீ அடிவயிற்றிலே, the fire the mother set in the belly, is read by tradition as the fire of grief she has left him by dying, or as the fire of hunger and birth itself that she gave by bearing him; both are Siddhar readings. மூள்க மூள்க, let it blaze, is the mourner's cry turned into consent, and the verse is sometimes read as the moment his renunciation becomes complete.

397.reading: It burns in the fire, it is burnt and turns to powder and ash, alas for me, sinner: the hand that cherished me and raised me, that dandled me so that the great bird would not fly away.
397.nuance: மாகக் குருவி பறவாமல், so that the sky-bird would not fly, is read as the mother guarding the infant's life (உயிர் as a bird that may leave the body), an image the Kural also uses; it may instead be a lullaby's bird. The verse watches a single part, the hand, go to ash.

398.reading: Has she burned, O skilful one of Sonagiri? Has she come to your feet? Has she forgotten me? The mother who bore me, who always looked to you and lay in longing for a boon.
398.nuance: சோணகிரி is Arunachala (Tiruvannamalai), so the mother is a devotee of that Lord, and the three questions run from the body (burned) to the soul (at your feet) to the bond (forgotten me). The last is the son's, not the ascetic's; the verse does not resolve it.

399.reading: She sat in state; she lay in the street; she was here yesterday and today has burned and become ash; without grieving 'come, all of you, to sprinkle the milk', all is Siva.
399.nuance: பாற்றெளித்தல் is the rite of sprinkling milk on the ashes the day after cremation, so the invitation refused is the last duty of mourning. எல்லாம் சிவமயம், everything is Siva, is the chapter's conclusion and the one line set apart in the text; it answers 398's questions by dissolving them, and it makes the mother's ash not less than Siva.

links.note: Arunagirinathar tells his own life from the embryo in his mother's body, born with desire and raised with love, to ask for love for the feet; Pattinathar tells his mother's ten months and her breast to ask in what birth he will see her. The same beginning is told from the child's side in one and from the mother's debt in the other.

The life as a bird: the Kural says body and life are friends only as a bird that flies off leaving its shell or nest; Pattinathar's mother dandled him so that the sky-bird would not fly away, that is, kept the life in the infant body. Pattinathar uses the Kural's figure for what the mother held back for a time.

The Kural says the world's greatness is that one who was here yesterday is not here today; Pattinathar says the same of his mother, enthroned, then in the street, then ash, and adds what the Kural does not, that the whole of it is Siva. The Kural's observation becomes a Saiva conclusion.

Tirumular's town wails, burns the man, bathes and stops thinking of him, which is the verse's reproach to the world; Pattinathar is the one who will not come to sprinkle the milk and does not grieve, and gives as his reason that all is Siva. The same refusal to mourn is folly in Tirumular's townsfolk and knowledge in Pattinathar.

430 asks what a mother who bathed, kept vigil, conceived, bore, raised and named a son can do if the son turns mad for God; 396 is that son at her pyre, counting the fire she set in his belly among the fires of the gods. The later verse states the mother's loss in general; this one lives it.

source_issues: The heading on 390 to 395 (தாயாருக்குத் தகனகிரியை செய்கையிற் பாடிய வெண்பா) and the metre labels on 396 to 399 are a modern editor's and not the poet's.
397 has the venba's third line run into the second after the dash (மாகக் குருவிபறவாமற்கோதாட்டியென்னைக்), so the line break is lost.
398 line 4 றன்னையயீன்றெடுத்ததாய் doubles the ய: read தன்னை ஈன்றெடுத்த தாய் (or என்றன்னை ஈன்றெடுத்த).
399 line 4 is spaced (எல்லாஞ் சிவமயமே யாம்) unlike the rest of the work, which is printed without word breaks; it may have been set apart by the editor.
